content.overview: Legitimate expectation protects a person who has been led to expect a benefit or a particular procedure by a public authority’s promise, practice or representation. It is rooted in fairness and Article 14 non-arbitrariness; it does not create an absolute right and cannot override statute or public interest properly weighed.
content.glance: Identify the representation or practice; test whether expectation is legitimate; ask whether denial is fair and whether public interest justifies departure; state the consequence (hearing or substantive protection where applicable).
content.study: Legitimate expectation may be procedural (expectation of a hearing or consultation) or substantive (expectation of a benefit). Indian courts recognise the doctrine as an aspect of fairness under Article 14. The expectation must be based on a clear representation, established practice or promise by a public authority. It yields to statute, and a change of policy may be justified by overriding public interest if the change is not arbitrary. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in Article 14 and the specific representation or practice.

sections.heading: Basis of the Expectation
sections.body: Clear representation, consistent practice or promise by a public authority.

sections.heading: Procedural Legitimate Expectation
sections.body: Expectation of notice, hearing or consultation before a decision adverse to the person.

sections.heading: Substantive Legitimate Expectation
sections.body: Expectation of a benefit or continuance of a policy; protected against arbitrary denial subject to public interest.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: Cannot override statute; yields to bona fide change of policy in the public interest; not an absolute vested right.

examples.title: Assured benefit withdrawn
examples.body: An authority publishes a scheme and assures applicants that qualifying persons will receive a benefit. It later withdraws the scheme without hearing after applications are invited. Procedural and possibly substantive legitimate expectation are engaged.

examples.title: Policy change with reasons
examples.body: A long-standing policy is changed for recorded public-interest reasons after affected persons are heard. The expectation may yield to the justified policy change.

hypotheticals.question: Does legitimate expectation create a vested right?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. It is a fairness doctrine; it does not create an absolute right and yields to statute and justified public interest.

hypotheticals.question: Is a mere hope enough?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The expectation must be based on a clear representation, practice or promise attributable to the public authority.

distinctions.title: Legitimate expectation vs promissory estoppel
distinctions.left: Fairness-based protection of expectation from public authority conduct
distinctions.right: Equity-based enforcement of a clear promise inducing reliance

misconceptions.trap: Legitimate expectation is an absolute right.
misconceptions.correction: It is a fairness doctrine subject to statute and justified public interest.

misconceptions.trap: Any disappointment of hope creates a claim.
misconceptions.correction: Only expectations founded on clear representation, practice or promise are protected.

cases.name: Food Corporation of India v Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries
cases.facts: Expectation arising from government tender/policy process.
cases.issue: Scope of legitimate expectation in administrative decision-making.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Legitimate expectation is a part of the rule of non-arbitrariness under Article 14; it does not create an absolute right.
cases.relevance: Leading Indian authority on legitimate expectation.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a legitimate-expectation problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the representation or practice. II. Test legitimacy of the expectation. III. Ask whether denial is fair / public interest justifies departure. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Representation identified; expectation characterised; fairness/public-interest analysis; precise relief.

examTips: State that it is not an absolute right.

enhancement.definition: Legitimate expectation protects a person led by a public authority’s representation or practice to expect a benefit or procedure, subject to fairness and public interest.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Expectation founded on clear representation or practice is protected against arbitrary denial under Article 14; it is not an absolute right.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The doctrine operationalises fairness when public authorities create expectations.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify representation; test legitimacy; weigh public interest.
keyTakeaways: Yields to statute and justified public interest.
